doc.title: Lou Donaldson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Using Ray Barretto's conga to steady the rhythm
summary: He says congas controlled the rhythm and that Latin jazz is just jazz with Latin rhythm.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: I’m going to move into another area. You were one of the first jazz group leaders to use a conga player, as you were describing with Ray Barretto on those Blue Note dates from 1957. I think you used the phrase just now, “straighten out the rhythm.” What exactly did you mean by that, and what...

Actually, I meant control. Now you can see today you’ve got these guys like Poncho Sanchez and a couple of more Latino musicians making a lot of money, because they put that beat with jazz. Because there’s no such thing as Latin Jazz. You can kiss that goodbye. That’s a misnomer. It’s jazz with Latin rhythm. That’s all it is. And when they keep that rhythm, which is the heart of the thinking in their music, they can sell the records. We could have done it ourselves if we’d kept our rhythm, with Kenny Clarke and Max... Those guys were shooting a little cocaine...shooting a little heroin and snorting a little cocaine—they didn’t want to swing any more. They wanted to take a solo. Most of the time, when somebody else is soloing. That’s what the problem is. That’s how they’re losing out.
But what was the value for you of having the conga player?
To steady down the rhythm. That’s all.
